common_name: Georgia Bush Velvet Bean (Non-Climbing Bush-Type Nitrogen-Fixing Cover Crop)

planting.note: Direct sow large seeds after soil is reliably above 65°F; Georgia Bush is a determinate, non-vining selection that stays compact rather than scrambling over fences and neighboring crops like typical climbing velvet bean strains.

directions: Georgia Bush traces back to a single bushy, non-climbing plant found and selected by a Georgia grower in a field of otherwise vining velvet beans, a spontaneous mutation that breeders and researchers across the South later carried forward because of the obvious management advantage of a velvet bean that holds its own ground instead of smothering everything nearby. Like other velvet beans it is an exceptionally vigorous warm-season legume that fixes large amounts of nitrogen and builds organic matter fast in hot, humid conditions, but its upright, clumping habit makes it far easier to work into row-crop middles, orchard floors, or garden beds where a sprawling vine would be unwelcome. All plant parts still carry the irritating silica-based trichomes typical of the species, so handle pods and foliage with gloves and long sleeves. Mow or turn in at flowering for the best balance of biomass and quick residue breakdown, and scarify or soak the hard seed coat before planting to speed germination.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Characterization of Velvetbean Germplasm
University of Florida IFAS — Mucuna Species for Cover Cropping

common_name: Lewis Guar (High-Yield Texas-Bred Drought-Tolerant Legume Cover Crop)

planting.note: Direct sow only once soil is reliably warm, since guar germinates poorly below about 70°F; Lewis is a fine-branching Texas cultivar bred for higher seed yield than older guar releases like Kinman.

directions: Lewis was developed in Texas from a cross of two breeding lines and has outyielded the long-standing Kinman cultivar in multi-location Texas seed trials, thanks in part to a finer-branching growth habit that packs more pod-bearing nodes onto each plant. As a legume it adds some nitrogen back to the soil, but its real value as a Gulf Coast and South Texas cover crop comes from its deep taproot and exceptional tolerance of heat and drought, letting it hold ground and suppress weeds on sandy, low-fertility soils through the hottest, driest stretch of summer when many other cover legumes struggle. It is strictly a warm-season annual that is killed outright by frost, so time sowing well after the last freeze and plan to mow or incorporate residue before cold weather returns. Rotate with a non-legume the following season if guar has been grown repeatedly on the same ground, since disease pressure can build in continuous guar plantings.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Research — Guar Variety Development
USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Guar (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba)
SARE — Alternative and Dryland Cover Crop Options

common_name: Catjang Cowpea (Erect Warm-Season Nitrogen-Fixing Pulse and Green Manure)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following the last frost; catjang's upright, bushy habit lets it be sown closer and more densely than sprawling vine-type cowpeas grown for the same cover-crop purpose.

directions: Catjang is a distinct botanical group within Vigna unguiculata, set apart from common cowpea and yardlong bean by its narrow, more or less erect cylindrical pods carrying an unusually high ovule count, and by a generally more upright, less sprawling plant habit than the vining cowpea types most often sold as Southern cover crops. It has long been grown through South and Southeast Asia for food, livestock forage, silage, and green manure, and performs the same quick nitrogen-fixing, weed-smothering role as other warm-season cowpeas when sown into hot Gulf Coast summer gaps. Its more compact, bushy growth makes it easier to manage at closer spacing than long-vining cowpea selections, while still tolerating the heat, humidity, and sandy, low-fertility soils typical of the region. Turn the crop in or mow it at flowering for the greatest nitrogen contribution to the following planting.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata)
SARE — Managing Cover Crops Profitably: Cowpeas
